The Honeywell Home TH6220U2000/U is a T6 Pro wall thermostat. It is rated for up to 2 heat and 2 cool.

Programmable. Setback on a schedule is where the savings actually come from on a system that runs daily. If the building empties on a predictable pattern, the schedule pays for the difference in price over a non-programmable unit; if it does not, it will not.

Where it sits in the range. Resideo builds these in tiers, and the tier number is the amount of control you get, not the build quality. T1 and PRO 1000 are single-stage and non-programmable — set it and leave it. T3 and PRO 3000 add a digital display and more staging. T4 and PRO 2000 add scheduling. T6 covers multi-stage and heat pump work, with a Smart version that adds Wi-Fi. T10 Pro is the top of the line, with RedLINK and remote room sensing. PRO 1000, PRO 2000 and PRO 3000 are the older names for the same tiers as T1, T4 and T3 — if you are matching what came out of the wall, the PRO number and the T number can be the same generation of product under two labels.

Before you order. Match the thermostat to the equipment, not to the room: count the heating and cooling stages the system actually has, and confirm whether it is a heat pump or a conventional system, because the two wire differently at the thermostat. A unit rated for more stages than you have will work; one rated for fewer will not run the equipment you own. If you are replacing a Honeywell Home unit, the part number carries over — Honeywell Home thermostats are made by Resideo, and the legacy numbering is the same.

The TH5110D1022 is a non-programmable thermostat from Honeywell Home.

A non-programmable thermostat holds one setpoint until someone changes it. That is the whole design, and it is the right design more often than the market admits: in a shop, a rental, a spare room or anywhere occupancy has no schedule, a programmable stat gets overridden permanently within a week and then behaves like this one with extra steps.

Where it hangs decides what it reads. A thermostat measures the air touching it and nothing else, so an interior wall about five feet up, out of direct sun, away from supply registers and doorway drafts, and clear of the back of a wall carrying hot water or flue pipe. Most complaints that a stat is “off by three degrees” are placement, not calibration — the stat is reading the truth about a spot nobody lives in.

These are also the straightforward answer to the C-wire problem. A smart thermostat needs a common wire to power itself continuously, and in an older house that wire is often not in the bundle — which turns a thermostat swap into a wire pull. A non-programmable stat does not draw a continuous 24 V supply for itself, so the wires already on the wall are usually the wires it needs.

If the stat has an adjustable heat anticipator, set it to the current stamped on the primary control rather than leaving it where it arrived. Too low and the burner shuts off early and the room never reaches setpoint; too high and it overshoots and then coasts cold. It is the one adjustment on a stat like this that changes comfort, and the one most often skipped.

Confirm the system type before ordering — low voltage, line voltage and millivolt thermostats look similar and are not interchangeable.

The Honeywell Home TH1110DH1003/U is a PRO 1000 wall thermostat. The case is the horizontal version — horizontal and the other orientation are electrically the same thermostat in a different body, so pick the one that matches the footprint and the wire opening already in the wall.

Non-programmable. One setpoint, changed by hand. That is the right choice for a rental, a shop, a space on a fixed occupancy, or any job where a schedule would just get overridden. Fewer things to explain at handover, and nothing to reprogram after a power event.

Where it sits in the range. Resideo builds these in tiers, and the tier number is the amount of control you get, not the build quality. T1 and PRO 1000 are single-stage and non-programmable — set it and leave it. T3 and PRO 3000 add a digital display and more staging. T4 and PRO 2000 add scheduling. T6 covers multi-stage and heat pump work, with a Smart version that adds Wi-Fi. T10 Pro is the top of the line, with RedLINK and remote room sensing. PRO 1000, PRO 2000 and PRO 3000 are the older names for the same tiers as T1, T4 and T3 — if you are matching what came out of the wall, the PRO number and the T number can be the same generation of product under two labels.

Before you order. Match the thermostat to the equipment, not to the room: count the heating and cooling stages the system actually has, and confirm whether it is a heat pump or a conventional system, because the two wire differently at the thermostat. A unit rated for more stages than you have will work; one rated for fewer will not run the equipment you own. If you are replacing a Honeywell Home unit, the part number carries over — Honeywell Home thermostats are made by Resideo, and the legacy numbering is the same.

The TL8230A1003 is a line-voltage thermostat from Honeywell Home for electric resistance heat — baseboard, convectors, radiant ceiling or panel heaters.

Line voltage is the distinction that matters here. A low-voltage thermostat switches a 24 V control circuit and lets a furnace or boiler do the work; a line-voltage thermostat carries the full heater current itself. They are not interchangeable, and a low-voltage stat wired to a baseboard circuit fails immediately.

This is a double-pole thermostat: it breaks both legs of the supply, so the heater is fully de-energized when the thermostat is satisfied or turned off. Double-pole is what most jurisdictions require on 240 V baseboard, and it is what makes the heater safe to work on with the thermostat off.

The programmable schedule lets the heat drop back when the room is empty and recover before it is used again. On electric resistance heat, where every watt is billed at full price, setback is the single largest saving available — there is no efficiency to improve, only run time to remove.

Match the voltage and the pole configuration to the heater circuit, and check the amperage of the heater against the rating of the thermostat. A thermostat sized below the load is the most common cause of a line-voltage stat failing in its first season.

Line voltage is the distinction that matters here. The TH135-01-B is a non-programmable thermostat from Honeywell Home, heat-only.

A non-programmable thermostat holds one setpoint until someone changes it. That is the whole design, and it is the right design more often than the market admits: in a shop, a rental, a spare room or anywhere occupancy has no schedule, a programmable stat gets overridden permanently within a week and then behaves like this one with extra steps.

Heat-only means there is no cooling changeover and no fan switch to get into the wrong position. On a boiler or a furnace with no air conditioning, that is one less thing for a tenant to set wrong.

Where it hangs decides what it reads. A thermostat measures the air touching it and nothing else, so an interior wall about five feet up, out of direct sun, away from supply registers and doorway drafts, and clear of the back of a wall carrying hot water or flue pipe. Most complaints that a stat is “off by three degrees” are placement, not calibration — the stat is reading the truth about a spot nobody lives in.

These are also the straightforward answer to the C-wire problem. A smart thermostat needs a common wire to power itself continuously, and in an older house that wire is often not in the bundle — which turns a thermostat swap into a wire pull. A non-programmable stat does not draw a continuous 24 V supply for itself, so the wires already on the wall are usually the wires it needs.

If the stat has an adjustable heat anticipator, set it to the current stamped on the primary control rather than leaving it where it arrived. Too low and the burner shuts off early and the room never reaches setpoint; too high and it overshoots and then coasts cold. It is the one adjustment on a stat like this that changes comfort, and the one most often skipped.

Confirm the system type before ordering — low voltage, line voltage and millivolt thermostats look similar and are not interchangeable.
